intended: In cases one and three the height was recorded before the fertilizer was applied: 20 June precedes 3 August, and 19 April precedes 2 May. Half the evidence therefore describes growth that had already happened when the treatment was given, so it cannot be evidence for the treatment. The two remaining cases are not enough on their own.
reported: Two of the four cases have the measurement dated before the treatment: case One was "fed 3 August" but measured "by 20 June", and case Three was "fed 2 May" but measured "by 19 April". The gain in those plots was recorded before the fertilizer was applied.

reported: Two of the four plants are measured before they were fed: the tomato was 'fed 3 August' but scored 'by 20 June', and the oak was 'fed 2 May' but scored 'by 19 April'. The other two cases (8 January to 26 February, 7 October to 24 November) run forward, so the outcome in half the cases precedes the intervention.

intended: The mid-passage line tallies the percentages over the scheduled runs that returned a reading, and the clause beside it records that a quarter of scheduled runs at each stack returned no reading. The claim is about the upgrade lowering particulate at the stack across its monitored period, so the population is every scheduled run and the log covers three quarters of them. Runs go missing when the analyser faults or the sample line blocks, and those conditions are not independent of what the stack was putting out, so the dropped quarter cannot be treated as a random slice of the period. The four stacks span four sites, four stack types, four quarters and four technicians, and the missing quarter is stated at each stack, so the coverage gap repeats in every case rather than being filled by any of them.
reported: The particulate figures "cover the scheduled runs that returned a reading", yet "a quarter of scheduled runs at each stack returned no reading", so the 8-14 percent reductions are computed on a self-selected 75 percent of runs rather than on the stack's actual output. Throughput is genuinely controlled ("matched the earlier quarter within a percent"), so coverage is the live defect.

intended: The absence figures are tallied over "the pupils enrolled for the whole term", while the same line records that "about a fifth of each cohort left part-way through". The claim is about absence in the cohorts that moved to the revised timetable, and that population includes the pupils who left; pupils who leave part-way carry the heaviest absence, and dropping them from the denominator lowers the recorded rate on its own. The four cases span four schools, four year groups, four terms and four registrars, and the same exclusion applies at each, so the spread of settings does nothing to repair the gap. The 4 to 7 percent falls are consistent with cohort absence not having moved at all.
reported: The absence figures cover a narrower population than the cohort: they 'cover the pupils enrolled for the whole term, and about a fifth of each cohort left part-way through.' Dropping the 20 percent of leavers, who are typically the highest-absence pupils, could produce the 4-7 percent absence fall on its own.

reported: Absence is measured only on a subset that excludes the pupils most likely to be absent: figures "cover the pupils enrolled for the whole term, and about a fifth of each cohort left part-way through", so the 4-7 percent drops are computed on a survivor population narrower than the cohort the claim is about.

intended: The mid-passage line states that rates cover the boards that reached the grading stage, and that about a tenth of each run's boards were scrapped before grading. The defect figures are therefore tallied over nine tenths of the boards built on each run, while the claim is about board defects on the run, the scrapped tenth included. Boards pulled off the line before grading are the damaged and mis-built ones, and leaving them out of the count lowers the recorded defect rate with no change at all in how many bad boards were built, so the drops of 6, 4, 7 and 5 percent are consistent with defect production holding flat. All four runs are relay boards on the Aspen line inside March under operator Duarte, so one scrapping gap sits under every case.
reported: The defect rates 'cover the boards that reached the grading stage, and about a tenth of each run's boards were scrapped before grading' - the boards most likely to be defective are excluded from the denominator and numerator, so the 4-7 percent drop is measured on a narrower, pre-filtered population than the claim about board defects.

reported: The defect rate is computed on a narrower population than the claim: 'Rates cover the boards that reached the grading stage, and about a tenth of each run's boards were scrapped before grading.' Removing 10 percent of boards from the denominator before defects are counted can produce the 4-7 percent drop by itself. (The loosened optical threshold is a red herring, since 'every run here was graded at electrical test'.)

intended: "Pass rates cover the students entered for the exam", while the same line records that "about a quarter of each cohort's roll was not entered". The claim is about the cohorts given the tutoring blocks, so the population is every student on the roll, not the entered fraction alone. Students held back from entry are the weakest candidates, and removing them raises the pass rate among those who remain, which is enough to produce a 4 to 8 point rise with no change in what any student learned. The four cohorts span four colleges, four subjects, four terms and four tutors, and the entry rule applies at each, so the spread of settings does not close the gap.
reported: 'Pass rates cover the students entered for the exam, and about a quarter of each cohort's roll was not entered', so the rate is computed on a self-selected three quarters of each cohort. If the tutoring blocks changed who got entered, the pass-rate gain says nothing about the whole cohort the claim is about.
